q: What is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea?
x: Pregnancy. A corpus luteum rescued by hCG keeps progesterone high, so the endometrium is not shed; that is why an hCG test comes first in every amenorrhea work-up.

w.Polycystic ovary syndrome: PCOS is the most common cause of chronic anovulation in women who are not pregnant, but pregnancy must be excluded before it is considered.
w.Hyperprolactinemia: High prolactin suppresses GnRH and is a classic cause, but it accounts for a minority of cases and is tested only after hCG.
w.Primary ovarian insufficiency: Ovarian insufficiency affects about 1 in 100 women before 40; it is diagnosed by high FSH once pregnancy is excluded.
w.Asherman syndrome: Intrauterine adhesions after curettage are a rare, history-driven cause with normal hormone levels.

pt.say: Step 1 of the work-up is the pregnancy test (hCG), because pregnancy is the most common cause.

q: By what age does absent menarche define primary amenorrhea in a girl with breasts?
x: Age 15. A girl with breast development who has not menstruated by 15 needs evaluation; with no breast development at all, evaluation starts at 13 because puberty itself is delayed.

w.Age 13: Thirteen is the threshold when breasts have not developed at all, which signals delayed puberty rather than isolated amenorrhea.
w.Age 12: Twelve is close to the average age of menarche in the United States, not a cutoff that triggers evaluation.
w.Age 16: Sixteen was an older threshold; current guidance evaluates at 15 so that causes such as outflow obstruction are found sooner.
w.Age 18: Waiting until 18 would delay the diagnosis of Turner syndrome, Müllerian agenesis and other treatable causes by years.

pt.say: The left branch header reads primary: no menses by age 15 in a girl who has developed breasts.

q: How long must menses be absent after regular cycles to define secondary amenorrhea?
x: 3 months. After regular cycles, three missed months define secondary amenorrhea; after irregular cycles the threshold is 6 months, because long gaps are already part of her pattern.

w.6 weeks: A 6-week delay usually means one late ovulation or an early pregnancy; it is too short to define a menstrual disorder.
w.6 months: Six months applies to women whose cycles were already irregular, not to someone who had regular periods.
w.12 months: Twelve months without menses after age 45 defines menopause, which is a different definition.
w.2 weeks: Two weeks late is common normal variation in the follicular phase and meets no definition.

pt.say: The right branch header reads secondary: none for 3 months after regular cycles.

q: Which symptom sets Kallmann syndrome apart from other causes of low GnRH?
x: Anosmia. GnRH neurons migrate from the olfactory placode alongside olfactory axons; when migration fails, the patient has both hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and no sense of smell.

w.Galactorrhea: Galactorrhea points to hyperprolactinemia, which suppresses GnRH through prolactin rather than through failed neuron migration.
w.Short stature: Short stature with ovarian failure suggests Turner syndrome, where FSH is high rather than low.
w.Hirsutism: Hirsutism points to androgen excess, as in PCOS or congenital adrenal hyperplasia, not to GnRH deficiency.
w.Cyclic pelvic pain: Cyclic pain with primary amenorrhea suggests blocked outflow, such as an imperforate hymen, with normal hormones.

pt.say: Under no breasts with low FSH, the figure lists Kallmann syndrome (anosmia): smell and GnRH fail together.

q: Which lab finding defines primary ovarian insufficiency before age 40?
x: High FSH on two occasions weeks apart, with low estradiol. Without follicles there is no estradiol or inhibin feedback, so the pituitary drives FSH into the menopausal range.

w.Low FSH with low estradiol: This pattern places the failure above the ovary, as in functional hypothalamic amenorrhea or pituitary disease.
w.High prolactin: High prolactin suppresses GnRH and lowers FSH, the opposite of the ovarian failure pattern.
w.High 17-hydroxyprogesterone: This marks 21-hydroxylase deficiency, a cause of androgen excess rather than ovarian failure.
w.Low TSH: A low TSH means hyperthyroidism, which can disturb cycles but does not define ovarian insufficiency.

pt.say: The box labeled high FSH before age 40 is primary ovarian insufficiency: the failed ovary sends no feedback.

q: Which three findings make up the female athlete triad?
o: Low energy, amenorrhea, low bone density
x: Low energy availability, menstrual dysfunction and low bone mineral density. Too little fuel for training slows GnRH pulses, estrogen falls, and bone resorption outpaces formation, so stress fractures follow.

w.Obesity, anovulation, hirsutism: This trio describes PCOS, an androgen-excess state with normal or high estrogen and preserved bone.
w.Galactorrhea, amenorrhea, headache: This trio suggests a prolactinoma, where prolactin suppresses GnRH and the mass can press on nearby structures.
w.Anosmia, amenorrhea, low FSH: This is Kallmann syndrome, a congenital GnRH deficiency present from birth rather than acquired through training.
w.Anemia, amenorrhea, fatigue: Anemia and fatigue can accompany heavy training, but the triad centers on energy deficit and bone density.

pt.say: The O branch names the female athlete triad: low energy availability, amenorrhea and low bone density, with slowed GnRH pulses lowering estradiol.

q: What does a withdrawal bleed after a progestin challenge show?
x: Estrogen is present and the outflow tract is open. Progestin withdrawal can only shed an endometrium that estrogen has already built, so the problem is anovulation, as in PCOS.

w.Ovarian failure with low estrogen: Ovarian failure leaves estrogen too low to build an endometrium, so progestin withdrawal produces no bleed.
w.Hypothalamic suppression of GnRH: Hypothalamic suppression lowers FSH and estradiol, leaving a thin lining that does not bleed after progestin.
w.Scarred endometrium from adhesions: Asherman adhesions replace the functional endometrium, so no bleed occurs even with estrogen priming.
w.Pituitary tumor lowering gonadotropins: A pituitary tumor that lowers gonadotropins also lowers estradiol, which predicts a negative challenge.

pt.say: In the progestin challenge box, bleed means estrogen present, outflow open, so the problem is anovulation.

q: Which criteria diagnose PCOS from two of three findings?
x: Rotterdam criteria: two of oligo- or anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound, after excluding thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia and nonclassic CAH.

w.Amsterdam criteria: Amsterdam criteria identify families with Lynch syndrome, which raises the risk of colon and endometrial cancer.
w.Jones criteria: Jones criteria diagnose acute rheumatic fever from carditis, arthritis, chorea and other signs after group A streptococcal pharyngitis.
w.Duke criteria: Duke criteria diagnose infective endocarditis by combining positive blood cultures, echocardiographic vegetations and minor clinical signs.
w.Ranson criteria: Ranson criteria estimate mortality in acute pancreatitis from age, laboratory values and fluid shifts.

pt.say: The polycystic ovary syndrome box lists the Rotterdam criteria: two of three findings (oligo-ovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries) once TSH, prolactin and 17-hydroxyprogesterone are excluded.

q: Why is free testosterone high in PCOS when total testosterone is only mildly raised?
x: Hyperinsulinemia suppresses the liver's production of sex hormone-binding globulin, so less testosterone is bound and the free, active fraction rises out of proportion to the total.

w.Adrenal DHEA-S is very high: A very high DHEA-S suggests an adrenal tumor; in PCOS it is normal or mildly raised and does not explain the free fraction.
w.Aromatase is overactive: More aromatase would convert testosterone to estradiol, lowering androgen levels rather than raising the free fraction.
w.Albumin is low: Albumin binds testosterone loosely and is normal in PCOS; SHBG is the carrier that insulin regulates.
w.5α-reductase is deficient: 5α-reductase deficiency lowers DHT and causes ambiguous genitalia in XY infants; it is unrelated to PCOS.

pt.say: Insulin resistance points to the liver box, which makes less SHBG, so free testosterone rises.

q: Which hormone test separates an adrenal from an ovarian androgen-secreting tumor?
x: DHEA-S. It is made almost entirely by the adrenal cortex, so a very high level points to an adrenal tumor, while very high testosterone with a normal DHEA-S points to the ovary.

w.Total testosterone: Testosterone is high with either tumor, so it signals a tumor but does not show which gland made the androgen.
w.LH: LH is suppressed by a tumor's androgen or estrogen output and gives no clue to the source.
w.Estradiol: Estradiol may rise from aromatization of tumor androgen in fat, which blurs rather than localizes the source.
w.Cortisol: Cortisol can be high with an adrenal carcinoma, but pure androgen-secreting tumors often leave it normal.

pt.say: The androgen source box separates the tumors: a very high DHEA-S points to an adrenal tumor, while very high testosterone with a normal DHEA-S points to an ovarian one.

q: Which letter of PALM-COEIN covers von Willebrand disease?
x: C, coagulopathy. Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder and classically causes heavy menstrual bleeding from menarche, often with nosebleeds or bleeding after dental work.

w.O, ovulatory dysfunction: Ovulatory dysfunction means anovulation with irregular, unpredictable bleeding, as in PCOS or the first years after menarche.
w.E, endometrial: Endometrial causes are local defects in hemostasis or repair within regular ovulatory cycles, with normal systemic clotting.
w.I, iatrogenic: Iatrogenic covers bleeding from anticoagulants, hormonal contraception or an IUD, not inherited disorders.
w.N, not otherwise classified: This group holds rare causes such as arteriovenous malformations and cesarean scar defects.

pt.say: In PALM-COEIN the C is coagulopathy: von Willebrand disease causes heavy bleeding since menarche, nosebleeds and bleeding after dental work.

q: What mediates the pain of primary dysmenorrhea?
x: Prostaglandins, mainly PGF2α, released as the secretory endometrium breaks down cause strong uterine contractions and ischemia; NSAIDs block their synthesis and are first-line treatment.

w.Ectopic endometrial implants: Endometriosis implants cause secondary dysmenorrhea, often with dyspareunia and infertility, and pain that worsens over years.
w.Endometrial glands within myometrium: Glands inside the myometrium define adenomyosis, a secondary cause with a boggy, enlarged uterus.
w.Fibroid degeneration: Fibroid degeneration causes acute pain, often in pregnancy, rather than monthly cramps from menarche.
w.Pelvic adhesions: Adhesions from surgery or infection cause chronic pelvic pain, a secondary cause with a structural lesion.

pt.say: At the end of the secretory phase, falling progesterone makes the endometrium release prostaglandins, which spasm the spiral arteries and cause the cramps of primary dysmenorrhea.

q: Which drug is first-line for ovulation induction in PCOS?
x: Letrozole. By inhibiting aromatase it lowers estrogen feedback, so FSH rises and drives follicle growth, and it gives more live births than clomiphene in PCOS.

w.Clomiphene: Clomiphene raises FSH by blocking hypothalamic estrogen receptors; it works but gives fewer live births than letrozole in PCOS.
w.Metformin: Metformin treats insulin resistance and helps metabolic risk but is a weak ovulation inducer on its own.
w.Spironolactone: Spironolactone treats hirsutism by blocking androgen receptors and must be stopped before conception.
w.Cabergoline: Cabergoline is a dopamine agonist that lowers prolactin; it restores ovulation in hyperprolactinemia, whereas prolactin is normal in PCOS.

pt.say: The ovulation column puts letrozole first in PCOS: an aromatase inhibitor that lowers estrogen feedback, so FSH rises and a follicle matures.

q: Which side effect is typical of clomiphene?
x: Visual disturbances, along with hot flashes, come from clomiphene's anti-estrogen action; blurring or flashing lights are a reason to stop the drug.

w.Hyperkalemia: Hyperkalemia is a risk of spironolactone, a potassium-sparing androgen blocker used for hirsutism.
w.Lactic acidosis: Lactic acidosis is the rare serious risk of metformin, especially with kidney failure or hypoxia.
w.Hirsutism: Hirsutism reflects androgen excess; clomiphene acts on estrogen receptors and does not raise androgens.
w.Galactorrhea: Galactorrhea follows high prolactin, as from dopamine antagonists, not from estrogen receptor blockade.

pt.say: The ovulation column lists clomiphene's side effects: hot flashes, visual disturbances and multiple births, from its anti-estrogen action.

q: What does free spill of contrast on hysterosalpingography show?
x: Patent fallopian tubes. Contrast pushed through the cervix spills into the peritoneal cavity only if the tubes are open; a dilated tube without spill is a hydrosalpinx.

w.Hydrosalpinx: A hydrosalpinx is a blocked, distended tube that fills with contrast but shows no spill into the peritoneum.
w.Intrauterine adhesions: The adhesions of Asherman syndrome appear as irregular filling defects inside the uterine cavity.
w.Bicornuate uterus: A bicornuate uterus shows a heart-shaped cavity with two horns; it concerns the cavity outline, not tubal spill.
w.Endometrial polyp: A polyp appears as a smooth filling defect in the cavity and can cause intermenstrual spotting.

pt.say: In the tubes column, free spill of contrast on hysterosalpingography means patent tubes, while a dilated tube with no spill is a hydrosalpinx.

q: What causes the fluid shift of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome?
x: VEGF-driven capillary leak. hCG from the trigger shot or an early pregnancy makes many luteinized follicles release VEGF, so fluid moves into the abdomen, causing ascites, hemoconcentration and thrombosis.

w.Ovarian torsion: Torsion is a complication of the enlarged ovaries, causing sudden severe pain, but it does not cause the fluid shift.
w.Ruptured ectopic pregnancy: An ectopic pregnancy causes pain and bleeding from tubal implantation, not ascites from leaky capillaries.
w.Tubo-ovarian abscess: A tubo-ovarian abscess follows pelvic infection with fever and a complex mass, not fertility drugs.
w.Theca lutein cyst rupture: Theca lutein cysts come from very high hCG, as in molar pregnancy; rupture causes pain but not systemic capillary leak.

pt.say: Gonadotropin treatment risks ovarian hyperstimulation: VEGF-driven capillary leak moves fluid into the abdomen, causing ascites, hemoconcentration and clots.
